stops.name: Röcken, the parsonage, the pastor's son
stops.campa: In the low parsonage of Röcken, hard by the twelfth-century church, the village pastor Karl Ludwig Nietzsche's first child is born on the fifteenth of October, the very birthday of King Friedrich Wilhelm IV, for whom the boy is named. The bells that toll for the king's day are said in the house to toll also for him, a coincidence the family reads as a small omen. He is baptized in the font his father tends, watched over by mother, grandmother, and aunts in a house already thick with piety and Lutheran learning.
stops.quote: The good fortune of my existence, its uniqueness perhaps, lies in its fatality: I am, to express it in the form of a riddle, already dead as my father, while as my mother I am still living and becoming old.
stops.quote_source: Ecce Homo, "Why I Am So Wise," §1

stops.name: Röcken, the father's death, the fatal fall
stops.campa: Karl Ludwig Nietzsche, ailing since a fall struck his head some months before, dies in the parsonage in his thirty-sixth year, leaving a widow, a boy not yet five, and an infant daughter. The village that had called him a saint among pastors now buries him beneath the church he served. Little Fritz, precocious and grave beyond his years, is said to have known beforehand in a dream that his father would come for him, a boy who from this hour walks, in his own later telling, already half a dead man's shadow.

stops.name: Naumburg, the house at Weingarten, exile from Eden
stops.campa: The parsonage must be vacated for the incoming pastor, and at Easter the widow Franziska removes her two children, her own mother, and two unmarried sisters-in-law to a rented house in Naumburg, on the street called Weingarten. Fritz will call the lost Röcken garden a paradise and Naumburg the world after the fall. Here, among five women and no man, the boy grows solemn, correct, devoted to his prayers, so priestly in bearing that the other boys nickname him 'the little pastor' and bring their disputes to him to judge.

stops.name: Naumburg, the little parson among women
stops.campa: At the Domgymnasium and in the household on Weingarten the boy reads and prays with a fervor that troubles no one yet, composes hymns, and weeps real tears reciting scripture aloud to his sister and cousins as though he were already in the pulpit his father left empty. Franziska and the aunts indulge and mold him: correctness, cleanliness, a horror of vulgarity. He is already, without knowing it, gathering the iron discipline that Schulpforta will sharpen and that his own hammer will one day be turned against.

stops.name: Schulpforta, admission to the Fürstenschule
stops.campa: At fourteen the boy is admitted on scholarship to Schulpforta, the ancient Cistercian cloister-school below Naumburg, harshest and most celebrated of the Saxon Fürstenschulen, the same iron walls that decades before formed Fichte, the goose-boy who became a philosopher. Here Nietzsche drills Greek and Latin among the sons of the Prussian gentry, poor and proud among them, and meets the lifelong friend Paul Deussen. The discipline is monastic, the loneliness deep, but the scholar within the little pastor is being forged.

stops.name: Schulpforta, confirmed beside Paul Deussen
stops.campa: In the school chapel Nietzsche is confirmed at the side of Paul Deussen, the two boys kneeling together before the altar in the rite that should seal a Lutheran life. He composes music and verse for the occasion in devout sincerity, still the pastor's son who wept over scripture at Naumburg. Within three years the same intellect, trained here to interrogate every text with philological rigor, will turn that rigor on the creed itself; but on this morning the confirmed boy believes he is entering, not leaving, the faith of his fathers.

stops.name: Schulpforta, graduation, "Fate and History" behind him
stops.campa: Six years of Schulpforta's Latin verses and Greek meters end in graduation. Already in a school essay of 1862, 'Fate and History,' the eighteen-year-old has argued that historical scholarship has quietly discredited Christianity's central claims, a thought he will not yet speak aloud at home. He leaves Pforta a brilliant philologist and a young man whose faith is a shell going hollow, bound for Bonn to study theology as his mother and dead father's calling still require of him.

stops.name: Bonn, theology becomes philology, the Franconia corps
stops.campa: Nietzsche matriculates at Bonn in theology and classical philology together, joins the Franconia fraternity, drinks and duels after the student fashion, and even takes a fencing scar to his nose. But the theology withers within one semester: to his devout mother's fury he abandons it entirely, unable to reconcile David Strauss's Life of Jesus and Feuerbach's demolitions with the creed of Röcken and Weingarten. He follows his teacher Friedrich Ritschl instead, transferring to Leipzig to become wholly a philologist.
stops.quote: If you wish to strive for peace of soul and pleasure, then believe; if you wish to be a devotee of truth, then inquire.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister Elisabeth, 11 June 1865

stops.name: Leipzig, old Rohn's bookshop, Schopenhauer found
stops.campa: New to Leipzig and following Ritschl, the twenty-one-year-old wanders into old Rohn's second-hand bookshop and picks up, by pure accident, a copy of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. He carries it home, throws himself onto the sofa, and does not rise until he has devoured all six hundred pages. Every line, he will say, screamed renunciation, denial, resignation: a mirror in which he saw the world, life, and his own mind reflected in terrifying grandeur. Philology has just acquired a rival: philosophy as a way of living dangerously.
stops.quote: Here every line screamed renunciation, denial, resignation, here I saw a mirror in which I caught sight of world, of life, and of my own mind in terrifying grandeur.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical fragment / letter to Carl von Gersdorff, 1865-66

stops.name: Leipzig, Ritschl's seminar, the philological prodigy
stops.campa: Under Ritschl's patronage Nietzsche's essays on Diogenes Laertius and the sources of Theognis mark him at once as the most gifted classicist of his generation. He founds a philological society with fellow students, corresponds intensely with Erwin Rohde and Carl von Gersdorff, and reads Schopenhauer and Kant by night against the grain of positivist philology by day. Ritschl privately calls him a phenomenon; the ordinary path of doctorate, then habilitation, then junior post, is about to be broken for him entirely.

stops.name: Naumburg, the cavalry, the fall from the saddle
stops.campa: Called to his year of Prussian military service, Nietzsche is posted to a mounted artillery regiment garrisoned near his mother's house at Naumburg. Vaulting into the saddle one March morning he strikes his chest hard against the pommel, tearing two muscles in his left side; he cannot walk unaided for months. The would-be soldier is invalided out on extended sick leave rather than formally discharged, and returns, weakened but relieved, to his books at Leipzig, the body already beginning the long rebellion against the mind that will mark his whole life.

stops.name: Leipzig, the parlor of the Brockhaus family, first meeting with Wagner
stops.campa: At the house of Hermann Brockhaus, Wagner's brother-in-law, the twenty-four-year-old philologist is introduced to Richard Wagner himself, in Leipzig incognito to visit his sister. The two talk long into the night of Schopenhauer, of German music, of the decadence of the age; Wagner plays passages from the still-unfinished Meistersinger. Nietzsche leaves electrified, certain he has met the living genius Schopenhauer's philosophy had seemed only to prophesy. A friendship that will remake and then unmake him has begun.
stops.quote: I was indescribably happy in those days, when I discovered Wagner!
stops.quote_source: Letter to Elisabeth Nietzsche, recalling 1868, in 1882
